title: Poller v. Columbia Broadcasting System, Inc. (1962)
summary: The Court’s cautious approach to summary judgment emphasized live testing of motive and intent in the antitrust dispute.
notes:
The supplied reading discusses Poller through an excerpt of commentary. It does not reproduce a full factual record or every issue in the opinion.

Poller owned WCAN, a UHF station in Milwaukee; he alleged CBS conspired to cancel WCAN's network affiliation, acquire competing station WOKY, and buy WCAN's equipment at distressed prices, in a treble-damage Sherman Act suit.

The decision was 5-4: Justice Clark wrote for the Court, and Justice Harlan dissented, joined by Justices Frankfurter, Whittaker and Stewart; the majority's oft-quoted rationale is that summary procedures should be used sparingly in complex antitrust cases where motive and intent play leading roles, the proof is largely in the hands of the alleged conspirators, and hostile witnesses thicken the plot.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff challenged CBS’s termination of its relationship with a television station as part of an antitrust conspiracy.
sections.Material Facts: The alleged scheme concerned cancellation of an affiliation and an effort to drive the plaintiff out of business. Motive and intent were central, and much of the evidence was held by persons accused of participating in the scheme. The defendants denied the prohibited purpose.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment and the court of appeals affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed.
sections.Issue: Was summary judgment appropriate on the showing concerning the alleged conspiracy and motive?
sections.Holding: The Court held that it was not and emphasized the need for caution in this setting.
sections.Reasoning: The opinion stressed the importance of live cross-examination where proof was concentrated among hostile witnesses and intent was disputed. The chapter uses it to explain the period of restrained use of summary judgment preceding the 1986 trilogy. That historical role must be preserved rather than converted into a categorical modern exemption for every case involving motive.

learning.why: The Court’s cautious approach to summary judgment emphasized live testing of motive and intent in the antitrust dispute.

topics.cp-summary-history: The Court urged caution where complex conspiracy and intent questions depended heavily on hostile witnesses.
topics.cp-access: The location of relevant proof in the alleged conspirators’ hands informed the concern about premature termination.
topics.cp-summary-judgment: Poller is the pre-1986 high-water mark of judicial hostility to summary judgment that the Celotex trilogy later cut back.
topics.cp-judge-jury: The Court reasoned that questions of motive and intent should be resolved by a jury after cross-examination rather than on affidavits.
